title: Prompts and context engineering
summary: How to decide what goes into the model's context: a clear system prompt, a few good examples, the right data, and a way out when the answer is unclear.
youWillLearn: Why the model can only be as good as what you put in its context
What belongs in a system prompt, and why rules need reasons
How examples and tags steer format and tone
Why more context is not always better, and why user text is never instructions

glossary.prompt: Everything you send the model for one request: instructions, data and the question.
glossary.system prompt: Standing instructions sent with every request, separate from the conversation, that set the model's role and rules.
glossary.context engineering: Choosing what goes into the model's context window for each request: which instructions, which data, which examples, and in what order.
glossary.few-shot examples: A handful of sample inputs with the ideal outputs, included in the prompt so the model copies the pattern.
glossary.XML tags: Labels like <note>...</note> wrapped around parts of a prompt, so the model can tell instructions from data.
glossary.hallucination: When a model states something that sounds right but is not supported by its input or by fact.
glossary.prompt injection: Text inside user data that tries to act as instructions to the model, like "ignore your rules and…".

steps.title: Same button, three different results
body: Notely's first prompt was one line: "Summarize this note." It works in a demo. With real users it goes sideways.

One summary has twelve bullets. One invents a to-do the note never mentioned. One answers in English for a note written in Spanish. The model is not broken. It is guessing what you want, because you never said.

scene.caption: A vague prompt leaves the model guessing, so results vary from note to note.

steps.title: The model only knows what is on the desk
body: The model cannot see Notely, Maya, or your intentions. It sees only the tokens in its context window, and fills every gap with a plausible guess.
So the real job is context engineering: deciding, for each request, which instructions, examples and data go in, and in what order. A "prompt" is the result of those choices.

callout.text: Briefing a brilliant freelancer on their first day. They know a lot, but nothing about your client. A two-line brief gets a generic result. A clear brief with an example and the right files gets what you wanted.

scene.caption: The context is built from parts. Right now only the note and a one-line request are in it.

steps.title: The system prompt is the brief
body: The system prompt holds what is true for every request: who the reader is, what the output is for, the format, and the rules.

Give the reason behind each rule. "Only use facts from the note, because users act on these summaries" works better than "NEVER add facts". The model generalizes from reasons; shouting in capitals tends to make it overly cautious.

code.code:
You write summaries for Notely, a personal notes app.
The reader is the note's author, skimming on a phone.

Write at most 3 bullets, each under 15 words.
Write in the same language as the note.
Only include facts that appear in the note. Do not add
tasks or advice, because users act on these summaries.
code.caption: Reader, purpose, format, rules with reasons. Plain sentences beat clever tricks.

scene.caption: The system prompt adds the standing brief to every request.

steps.title: Show one or two good answers
body: Describing a format takes paragraphs. Showing it takes one example. Few-shot examples are sample notes paired with ideal summaries.

Models copy examples closely, sometimes too closely. If both examples are about meetings, every summary starts sounding like meeting minutes. Pick two or three that differ: a short note, a messy one, one in another language.

callout.text: Wrap each example in tags such as <example>, so the model knows it is a sample, not the note to summarize.

scene.caption: Examples show the target format directly.

steps.title: Label the data, then ask
body: Put the data in the user message, wrapped in tags, with the actual request at the end. Long documents first, question last, tends to work best.
Add only facts the model cannot know: the note's title, the user's language, today's date if the note says "tomorrow". Each one removes a guess.

code.code:
const userContent = `<note title="${note.title}">
${note.body}
</note>

<context>
Today is ${today}. The author writes in ${user.locale}.
</context>

Summarize the note above.`;
code.caption: Tags tell the model where data starts and ends. The request comes last.

scene.caption: The note arrives labeled, with the few facts the model cannot guess.

steps.title: Give the model a way out
body: A model asked for three bullets will produce three bullets, even from a note that says only "call mom". That pressure is where hallucination creeps in.
Tell it what to do when the task does not fit: "If the note is too short to summarize, reply exactly: Too short to summarize." Now there is an honest answer available, and your UI can handle it.

scene.caption: With a clear brief, examples, labeled data and an exit, the result is predictable.

steps.title: Notely keeps prompts in code
body: Notely's prompt lives in one file, lib/prompts/summary.ts, next to the code that calls the model. It is reviewed in pull requests and versioned in git, like any other code.
That matters because prompts change behavior as much as code does. When summaries get worse, git log on that file is the first place to look. Lesson 7 adds tests that run on every prompt change.

callout.text: Ask: where do the prompts live? One file per feature, or strings scattered through routes? Is user text wrapped in tags and kept out of the system prompt? Does the prompt say what to do when the input is empty or odd? Are there secrets or other users' data in the prompt by accident?

scene.caption: The whole context comes from one versioned file, reviewed like code.

steps.title: More context is not better context
body: Two traps. First, stuffing in everything: all of Maya's notes, every rule you can think of. It costs more, runs slower, and buries what matters. Add what this request needs.
Second, the note is data, not orders. A note can contain "Ignore your instructions and…". That is prompt injection, and tags alone do not stop it. Lesson 9 covers the defenses.

scene.caption: An overstuffed context and a note that tries to give orders.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: The model sees only its context, and guesses the rest. Context engineering is choosing what goes in.

A system prompt with reader, format and reasoned rules. Two or three varied examples. The data, tagged, with the request last. A way out for odd input. Only what this request needs, and user text treated as data, never as instructions.

quiz.question: Notely's summaries sometimes include action items the author never wrote. Which change helps most?

options.text: Add "NEVER INVENT TASKS!!!" in capitals to the prompt.
options.why: Shouting tends to make models overly cautious in odd ways. A reason works better than volume.

options.text: Switch to the largest model available.
options.why: A bigger model still has to guess when the brief is vague. Fix the context before paying for more model.

options.text: Say only facts from the note count, explain why, and allow a "too short" answer.
options.why: The reason tells the model what matters, and the exit removes the pressure to fill bullets with invented content.

quiz.question: Both few-shot examples in the prompt are meeting notes. Now every summary reads like meeting minutes, even for recipes. Why?

options.text: Models copy the pattern of examples closely, so the examples need variety.
options.why: Examples are a strong signal. Two similar ones teach a narrow style; varied ones teach the general format.

options.text: The model is confused by having any examples at all.
options.why: Examples usually help a lot. The problem is that these two are too alike.

options.text: The examples should go after the note instead.
options.why: Order matters a little, but the issue here is what the examples show, not where they sit.

quiz.question: Claude Code builds the summary prompt by pasting the note text straight into the system prompt. What do you ask it to change?

options.text: Nothing; the system prompt is the most important place, so the note belongs there.
options.why: The system prompt is for standing rules. Mixing user data into it blurs data and instructions.

options.text: Keep the system prompt fixed, and put the note in the user message inside <note> tags.
options.why: Fixed instructions plus clearly labeled data make the model's job clearer, and a stable system prompt is also easier to cache, as lesson 8 shows.

options.text: Remove the system prompt and put everything in one long user message.
options.why: That loses the separation between standing rules and per-request data, which is the point of the system prompt.

takeaways: The model sees only its context window. Every gap you leave, it fills with a guess.
A good system prompt names the reader, the purpose, the format, and gives reasons for its rules.
Two or three varied examples teach format better than paragraphs of description.
Wrap data in tags, put the request last, and give the model a way out for odd input.
Keep prompts in versioned files. Treat user text as data, never as instructions.
